industrial_frontier.quest.defence.cannon: Large-calibre weapons here are assembled from blocks: barrel, breech, carriage, shell and a way to feed it. That is construction, not crafting.
Hence the role: artillery defends a place. It does not travel with you, it demands planning and a prepared position, but it solves problems hand weapons cannot.
Powder, metal and machining precision must already be in serial production by then. A cannon tests your factory, not your courage.
Artillery is a structure, not an item
When hand weapons are not enough
industrial_frontier.quest.defence.discip: First: death here is a logistics loss, not an instant rollback. Your things stay where you fell, and the walk back can outlast the fight.
Second: do not carry on a scouting run what you are not ready to lose. A field kit and a work kit are different kits.
Third: every faction operation comes with a warning and a negotiation window. Fighting is the last option, not the only one.
Fourth: repairing is cheaper than rebuilding. That is priced into gear on purpose.
Four rules that are cheaper learned in advance
industrial_frontier.quest.defence.firear: Firearms are never handed out before powder chemistry — that is a written pack ban, and it applies to recipes, quest rewards, trade and loot alike.
The key difference from a sword: a gun has a cost per shot. Ammunition must be produced, which means one more supply line that can fail at the worst moment.
So firearms here do not replace melee, they answer a different question. A sword costs nothing once forged; a gun needs a factory behind it.
A cartridge is a production consumable
Understand the cost of a shot
The pack ships three separate combat mods, and that is not a pile: each holds its own rung. Melee and armour work from day one, firearms appear after powder chemistry, heavy weapons sit beyond hand-held fighting entirely.
One rule, strictly held: gear never outruns production. You cannot find in a chest what you cannot yet build — which is why loot in other people's structures was stepped down rather than left alone.
The practical consequence: your fighting strength grows with your factory. If combat has you stuck, the answer is almost always in production, not in hunting for a better chest.
Weapons arrive with industry, not before it
A hit is no longer a click on a target. Weapons have a reach shape: an axe sweeps an arc and catches several foes, a spear reaches further but only ahead, a dagger is fast and weak.
So position matters. Standing in a crowd with a spear is a mistake; backing into a corridor with an axe is another. You pick the weapon for the situation, not for the damage number in the tooltip.
Knight armour gives real early protection and costs accordingly. That is a fair trade: you spend metal that could have gone into a machine.
Better Combat changes the swing itself
Melee: facing matters more than clicking
industrial_frontier.quest.defence.struct: Five structure mods ship here: biome-fitting villages and towns, reworked vanilla builds, ruins, towers and dungeons. The world is no longer empty field between your base and your mine.
This is not only scenery. Structures are a source of early materials, a landmark on the map and a place where you can meet somebody else's squad. Scouting stopped being pointless.

Worth knowing separately: their loot was audited and stepped down to match the gear ladder. Netherite became diamond, diamond became iron, and elytra, totems and enchanted apples were removed outright. What you find no longer cancels what you build.
Some four hundred structures, and not all are friendly
Find a structure and search it
The world around you is inhabited
industrial_frontier.quest.diplomacy.affi: You can be deeply respected by a faction without belonging to it. You can be formally enrolled without being trusted. You can leave and keep a special standing.
This is why reputation, affiliation and combat recognition are stored separately and are not derived from one another.
In practice: membership gives you a catalogue and access, respect gives you prices and tolerance, and recognition decides whether they shoot.
industrial_frontier.quest.diplomacy.epoc: Your team has a single technology level from P0 to P9. It decides how factions are armed, which bases they build and which operations against you are possible.
It does not grow from days lived, a lucky find or a dimension visited. Only a passed milestone raises it, and every raise is recorded.
Hence a simple consequence: the world will not get more dangerous while you stand still. And it will not lag behind if you raced ahead.
Not world days, but the level you reached
industrial_frontier.quest.diplomacy.intr: The district is already occupied. Six factions pursue their own interests: some build cities, some move cargo, some see your industry as a threat.
They do not appear on a timer and do not attack out of nowhere. Their behaviour follows what you built, what you trade and how you answered before.
This chapter explains the rules of dealing with them. There is no plot here yet — there are states that a plot will later be made of.
Six factions and one team of yours
Understand that the outside world reacts to you
industrial_frontier.quest.diplomacy.loot: A faction base holds what fits its era: blueprints, intelligence, damaged assemblies, components, optics, tools and currency.
Finished weapons of later eras are not there and never will be. Taking a base does not skip your industry — it gives knowledge and materials that speed it up.
Base tier is capped by era too: no military complex appears in an early world, however many days pass.
Learn the faction base loot rule
industrial_frontier.quest.diplomacy.oper: An operation never starts with a strike. First recon, then a warning, then a negotiation window — and only then action, if talking failed.
Every operation has a concrete objective: cut a route, take a share from a utility node, stop one line. The objective is never "destroy the base".
Any outcome is followed by recovery and a pause. A repeat operation does not start immediately, and offline raids do not happen at all.
industrial_frontier.quest.diplomacy.reco: A failed operation costs resources, time and reputation — but not progress. Your base is not razed irreversibly, and production comes back with repairs.
That is deliberate: the difficulty here lives in designing lines, not in the risk of losing a hundred hours to a single fight.
If something did break beyond repair, the chapter "90 — Help and recovery" describes how to diagnose and restore it.
Losing does not end the run
Know what to do after a failed operation
industrial_frontier.quest.diplomacy.repu: Each faction has its own scale from -100 to 100. It changes only from your actions: a contract fulfilled, a refusal, a broken treaty, help in defence.
Seven tiers: sworn enemy, hostility, distrust, neutrality, respect, alliance and special standing. The tier decides what they will discuss with you at all.
Killing one fighter does not make a faction your enemy forever. But a one-off gift does not buy an alliance either — reputation accumulates.
From sworn enemy to special standing
Review how all six factions regard you
industrial_frontier.quest.diplomacy.trea: Almost any operation can be closed with a treaty: a delivery, a toll, an exchange of intelligence or joint defence.
A treaty is not surrender. It fixes the price of the question and suspends repeat demands for a time, which often beats a single victory.
Breaking a treaty costs more reputation than refusing to sign one. Promising and failing is worse than an honest refusal.
Understand when a treaty beats a fight
industrial_frontier.quest.elements.carbo: Carbon works in three roles at once. It burns as fuel, takes oxygen from oxides as a reductant, and serves as the base of polymers.
Hence coke: it is made not for heat but for chemical work in metallurgy. Coke gas and tar go on into chemistry, not into nothing.
Later the same carbon returns as activated filter media — the same element cleans what it helped pollute.
Follow the three roles of carbon
industrial_frontier.quest.elements.chlor: Electrolysis of brine gives chlorine, hydrogen and alkali at the same time. Picking only one product is impossible.
This is the best lesson in the Academy: chemistry cannot be planned around a single substance. You want chlorine — hydrogen and alkali appear anyway, and they need a receiver.
Chlorine goes into water treatment and polymers, hydrogen returns to ammonia, alkali neutralises acids. The circle closes on the earlier cards.
Assign a consumer to each of the three products
industrial_frontier.quest.elements.index: Every substance in the pack has a passport: world source, allowed forms, purity classes, process owners, era, consumers, waste, renewability and the Russian term.
If you do not know where to get a substance or where to put its waste, the answer is in the passport. The chapter 70 — Material passports covers its fields in detail.
The rule to carry away: every stream has an owner and a receiver. A substance without a receiver is a design error, not rubbish.
Open any substance passport and read its fields
How to read a substance passport
industrial_frontier.quest.elements.intro: This is not a progression line. You come here when you need to understand where a substance comes from and where it goes afterwards.
There are no hand-in tasks and no rewards that break the economy. There are process cards and an explanation of why a chain is built the way it is.
Every cycle is described the same way: source, refining steps, product, side streams, consumers. If a side stream has nowhere to go, the chain is designed wrong.
A reference, not a required chapter
Understand what the Academy is for
industrial_frontier.quest.elements.nitro: Nitrogen is taken straight from air, combined with hydrogen into ammonia, oxidised into nitric acid — and from there three branches diverge.
The first feeds the city with fertiliser. The second gives explosives. The third goes into P7 rocket chemistry.
The order is not arbitrary: fertiliser pays the line back sooner, so agronomy opens before ammunition, not for story reasons.
Follow the path from air to fertiliser
industrial_frontier.quest.elements.nucle: Uranium travels a long road: concentrate, leaching, purification, reactor grade, isotope separation, fuel fabrication.
The road does not end at the reactor. Irradiated fuel is cooled, reprocessed and partly returned — the rest becomes accounted waste with long-term storage.
This is the one chain in the pack where an open loop is not merely suboptimal but unacceptable: this waste can be neither burned nor buried.
The one chain that must close
Follow the fuel cycle through to disposal
industrial_frontier.quest.elements.purit: The same substance exists in six classes: raw, technical, chemical, electronic, reactor and aerospace purity.
Each next step costs energy and produces waste. Reactor-grade uranium is not obtained at once — it is refined, and at every step part of the mass goes sideways.
Practical conclusion: never take purity higher than the recipe requires. An extra step is spent energy and extra waste you must also place somewhere.
Six classes, not good and bad
Tell the six purity classes apart
industrial_frontier.quest.elements.silic: Silicon is the first material where the purity class decides everything. Technical purity suits glass, electronic purity suits wafers, and several refining steps sit between them.
Hence the clean room: dust landing on a wafer ruins it entirely. That is not a decorative requirement, it is a process condition.
Electronics ties everything else together: without it there are no LV machines, no automation and no P5 digital factory.
Understand why electronics needs a clean room
industrial_frontier.quest.elements.sulfu: Sulfur comes from minerals and from cleaning petroleum fractions. Its main product is sulfuric acid, the workhorse of all industrial chemistry.
The acid goes into etching, batteries, ore processing and fertiliser. One line feeds four industries — which is why it is built first.
The acid loop is closed, not dumped. That is safety, economy and the first real return stream of your factory at once.
Find four consumers of sulfuric acid
industrial_frontier.quest.elements.water: Raw water suits cooling and construction. Technical water has been filtered and is accepted by chemistry. Drinking water passes one more stage and is what the city needs.
Effluent always appears — it is not optional. It splits into sludge, biogas and process water, and every stream has a receiver.
The return is bounded on purpose: some water is always lost to evaporation and washing, so raw make-up is permanent. A perpetual loop does not exist.
Separate the three water classes and the effluent
industrial_frontier.quest.factions.bases: Each of the six factions has its own builds out there, matched to its trade: a roadside camp for the caravans, a working with a camp for the industrialists, a tower for the watchers.
They are rare — roughly one per forty-eight chunks. An event, not scenery along the road.
When you first arrive, the base wakes up: an envoy appears and the base tier is computed from your epoch. Early on that is a camp, not a military complex, even if the world is a thousand days old.
Findable simply by walking far enough
Their bases stand in the world
industrial_frontier.quest.factions.intro: Your standing is shown by /if_threat status: epoch, relations with all six factions, active treaties and the things they remember about you.

A specific dossier comes from /if_threat faction plus its name: what it does, how it fights, what it counts as victory, who it calls friends and who it openly fights. It also lists what it is currently willing to discuss.
How far the world has moved is shown by /if_threat growth. Factions match your epoch, not the age of the world: their bases and gear grow with you.
Three commands that answer every question
Where to look at all this
industrial_frontier.quest.factions.opera: An operation starts only if your standing with someone has fallen below minus eleven. At neutral or better, nobody is planning anything against you.

Then, step by step: first they study you, then they announce intent, then a four-minute negotiation window opens. You can settle with /if_threat operation negotiate or through an envoy — the operation is called off and standing rises.

If you stay silent, a squad arrives — at a distance, not behind your back. Any outcome is followed by recovery and an hour of cooldown. To see what is happening right now, use /if_threat operation status.
Warning, negotiation window, and only then a squad
industrial_frontier.quest.factions.reput: Standing never shifts for no reason. Every change carries a cause from a known list, shown alongside the number: not 'minus eighteen' but 'killed a faction civilian'.
Causes that count once are marked as such. The same conversation will not earn respect twice, while trade adds a little at a time, steadily.
Notable deeds travel. Allies of the wronged faction learn half of it, its enemies a third with the sign flipped. Small things are not retold to anyone.
Fifteen reasons, each of them named aloud
industrial_frontier.quest.factions.talks: An envoy stands at the base. Click them and a conversation opens: you can ask who they are, or move on to a treaty.

Which treaties appear depends on standing. Truce and trade are almost always available; alliance and joint defence only show up past forty-one points of respect. No button means you are not trusted that far yet.
The server decides this, not the politeness of your phrasing. You cannot ask an enemy for an alliance — not because they refuse, but because that conversation does not exist.
A missing button is also an answer
industrial_frontier.quest.factions.treat: A truce suspends hostile operations. A trade pact opens the whole catalogue. Tribute lowers pressure while it is paid but earns no respect. An alliance grants mutual defence and somebody else's enemies along with it. Joint defence sends a squad when you are hit.
You sign either through the envoy conversation or with /if_threat treaty sign plus faction and type. To see what exists, use /if_threat treaty list.
Breaking one costs forty points and is recorded as a permanent fact. It is the only action in the pack with no cheap way out: a treaty broken once is remembered, and trade will not wash it off.
Five kinds, and one of them stops operations
industrial_frontier.quest.help.index.des:
§6Do not repair at random§r
First identify the layer: a JEI recipe, quest condition, team progress, datapack/resource-pack loading, or a script error in the log.

§6Safe order§r
Preserve the state, reread the exact condition, inspect the recipe and item, wait one detection cycle, and then collect the log. Recovery commands come only after the cause is known.
§6Clear the search§r
Empty JEI's search box and check for an active mod filter. Then press R or U directly over the item in your inventory.

§6Check the process type§r
Some outputs come from machines rather than a crafting table. Review category tabs and note the machine, voltage, temperature, and duration.

§6If an authored recipe vanished§r
Record the item ID and expected recipe ID. Search `latest.log` for `KubeJS` and `industrial_frontier`. Do not add a second recipe tweaker: that turns one fault into two sources of truth.
industrial_frontier.quest.help.jei.title: JEI Shows Nothing
industrial_frontier.quest.help.latest_lo:
§6Location§r
After reproducing the issue, close the game normally and open the profile's `logs` folder. Send `latest.log` from that same run.

§6Keep the context§r
Send the complete file. The visible error often appears after its cause, while the mod list and early datapack messages are essential context.

§6Privacy§r
A log should not contain passwords or tokens. Warn separately if a private server address is sensitive, but do not remove arbitrary technical lines.
industrial_frontier.quest.help.not_count:
§6Read the verb§r
“Have” checks inventory, “submit” may consume, “visit” checks a dimension, and a checkmark needs manual confirmation. These conditions do not update in the same way.

§6Refresh honestly§r
Place the required item in normal inventory, wait up to two seconds, then reopen the book. For tag tasks, verify the exact item ID.

§6Do not hide the defect§r
Do not administratively complete a required quest before preserving the log and reproduction steps. A green checkmark without evidence conceals the broken condition.
§6Cause first§r
Administrative quest completion is acceptable only after the log is saved and the player demonstrably met the real condition while detection failed.

§6Smallest change§r
Repair one quest ID for one team. Never grant future-era items, raise `tech_epoch`, or alter reputation through a scoreboard.

§6Record the action§r
Keep the Build ID, team UUID, quest ID, cause, command, and result after relog. If the build card does not define a recovery procedure, stop and send the log to Codex.
industrial_frontier.quest.help.report.de:
§6Minimum evidence§r
State the Build ID, singleplayer or multiplayer, new or existing world, exact steps, expected result, and actual result. Attach `latest.log` and one interface screenshot.

§6A useful reproduction step§r
Write “placed eight birch logs in the outer crafting slots; output remained empty”, not “crafting is broken”. One exact example lets us repair both recipe and explanation.
industrial_frontier.quest.help.team.desc:
§6Check membership§r
Open FTB Teams and confirm everyone sharing a base is on the same team. A player who joined after completion may need quest data to resynchronise.

§6What to report§r
Include the affected player, team name, who completed the condition, when the other player joined, and whether the mismatch survives a relog. Never edit the scoreboard to repair it.
industrial_frontier.quest.marathon.energ: Steam. Cheap, forgiving, runs on coal that is everywhere. You pay in volume: boiler, water, fuel and the room for all of it. Good until consumption grows.
Combustion engine. More compact and stronger than steam, but it needs fuel chemistry and its rhythm: refining stops, the factory stops. Good once the oil line exists and is stable.
Gas turbine. The best return among thermal sources for the same footprint, and the most demanding on supply. You build it when you have something to feed it constantly, not when you want more power.

Isotope source. Tiny, eternal and very weak. It never powers a factory — it powers what must never lose power: control, comms, emergency lighting. The only option here that does not compete with the others.
Pick the source that fits your rhythm, not your ambition
industrial_frontier.quest.marathon.final: The Dyson swarm tests scale. It cannot be built alone: it needs a production line for satellites, constant launches and a repair line. An abandoned sphere decays — the only structure in the pack that punishes forgetfulness.

The colony on Proxima b tests autonomy. Air, water, food and production must work on site; regular food deliveries from Earth do not count. This is the hardest exam: nearly the whole eight-epoch chain repeated on an alien planet.
You may build both, either one, or neither. These are two different finales, not two halves of one, and neither closes the other off.
Choose a finale or decline both
industrial_frontier.quest.marathon.intro: The rest of the book answers "how to do it right". This chapter answers a different question: "what to choose between".

The pack has five real forks. Each has several working paths, and none is better in general — they are better or worse under specific conditions: how much space you have, how much attention, what you already built.
Nothing unlocks here and nothing is granted. You come in when the fork is already in front of you and a decision is due.
A comparison handbook, not a progress line
Come here when a choice is due
industrial_frontier.quest.marathon.logis: Train. The only way to move a lot, far, over land. It costs rails, signals and planning, but one consist replaces dozens of trips. Not worth it on a short leg: acceleration and braking eat the gain.
Barge. Cheaper than a train where water already runs, useless where it does not. Slower, but needs neither track nor junctions.
Pipe and belt. Best over short distances and inside a shop. Beyond the base they become kilometres of infrastructure with nobody to maintain them.

ME network. It removes the routine of searching and counting, but creates no material and crosses no distance for free. It dies with the power. It goes on top of physical logistics, not instead of it — that is written as its own quest in the fifth-epoch chapter.
Trains, barges, pipes or a network
Split the four layers by distance
industrial_frontier.quest.marathon.nucle: Civil reactor. Assembled like a machine: vessel, fuel, coolant, turbine. Behaviour is predictable, mistakes cost resources. This is the workhorse of the city grid, and most players need nothing else.

Channel-type RBMK. Assembled column by column, and its behaviour depends on what you placed in every cell. It gives more, runs away faster than you can walk to the console, and demands a remote panel before the first startup.
The difference is not power but currency. The first takes materials, the second takes attention. Building both makes sense only if the process itself interests you: either one feeds the city.
Decide what you are willing to pay with
industrial_frontier.quest.marathon.space: The short path: three tiers of ready-made motor. Build, fuel, fly. It is entirely sufficient and reaches every planet of the programme — the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Venus and Proxima b.
The deep path: the engine designer. Combustion chamber, injector head, turbopump, nozzle — the engine is designed, not bought. Ninety-seven sequenced assemblies, hours of work.

The deep path leads to low orbit and the station, the short one to the planets. Not opening the designer is a legitimate decision, not skipped content: you lose nothing except the designing itself, which is the whole reason to open it.
A ready motor or your own engine
Decide whether the engine itself interests you
industrial_frontier.quest.mastery.boring: The pack has a rule: any mass component is automated before it becomes mass. By the late game that becomes the player's own rule.
The test is simple. If an action repeats a third time and you already know how it ends, that is not play, that is work. Automating it is cheaper than enduring it.
Space specifically: a run you fly by hand for thirty units of cargo never pays back. Either it is automatic, or that material is not needed.
If you are doing it by hand a second time, automate it
Find the action you are repeating for the third time
industrial_frontier.quest.mastery.expand: The most expensive late-game mistake is a shop built exactly to size. It works until you need twice as much, and then demolishing is easier than extending.
The cheap cure: leave an aisle and run the power and logistics bus with headroom. Empty space costs nothing; rebuilding a working shop costs everything.
The second cure: identical modules. Ten identical lines are easier to maintain and extend than one large one with a unique layout.
Leave room for the second row from the start
Leave expansion room before you need it
industrial_frontier.quest.mastery.handov: A distributed factory outlives breaks from the game. Coming back after a month and working out your own layout is a separate task, and the better you built, the harder it is.
The cheap cure: signs at shop entrances and on buffers. What is made here, where it comes from, where it goes. Three lines per shop.
The expensive but better cure: identical modules and a predictable layout. A scheme you can read at a glance needs no notes at all.
In a month you will not remember
Label the shops before you take a break
This chapter is optional. Nothing here unlocks anything: you come in when the factory is already built and has started behaving differently than intended.
Everything below is operating practice. How to tell where it stopped. How to size a reserve. How to expand without rebuilding half of it. How not to turn space into tedious work.
One rule holds for the whole chapter: a distributed factory fails quietly. Everything else is a way of hearing the failure before it reaches you as an empty store.
An operations handbook, not a progress line
Open this chapter when the factory starts behaving oddly
industrial_frontier.quest.mastery.power_: When power runs short, what goes dark is not the least important thing but whatever sits farther along the cable. Cure it in advance: separate critical supply from bulk.
Critical means life support, reactor cooling, control, and anything whose restart costs more than the downtime. Everything else may go dark.
The split is done once and saves you many times. Especially on planets where restarting a frozen line means another trip from Earth.
Shed load by importance, not by cable order
Separate critical supply from bulk supply
industrial_frontier.quest.mastery.reserv: Reserve is sized not by output but by how long it takes you to notice a problem and reach it. At the next base that is minutes; on another planet, hours or days.
The formula is simple: what the line consumes during your travel and repair time. Anything above that is frozen material, anything below is downtime.
That is why reserves on interplanetary legs are always larger than terrestrial ones — not caution but distance expressed in materials.
Size it by response time, not by throughput
Recalculate the reserve on an interplanetary leg
industrial_frontier.quest.mastery.where_: A long chain has a convenient property: it stops from the far end. While production runs, buffers before the broken section fill up and those after it drain.
So look not where the resource ran out but where it piled up. The first non-empty buffer along the chain sits right before the fault.
Practical consequence: a buffer should not be the largest but the most visible. An hour's capacity you can read at a glance beats a week's capacity nobody ever opens.
Look for the first non-empty buffer
Locate a fault by the first non-empty buffer
industrial_frontier.quest.oil.crusher.de: The same domain brings large block-built machines: a crusher, a blast furnace, a metal press. They assemble as structures and run on ordinary power.
Their niche is bulk throughput of simple processing. Where GregTech wants precise setup and its own casings, these give rough productivity at an understandable price.
At the seam between epochs they are often the better pick: a blast furnace covers your steel needs long before you reach industrial smelting lines.
industrial_frontier.quest.oil.crusher.su: Crusher, blast furnace and other structures
industrial_frontier.quest.oil.distillati: The distillation tower splits crude into fractions. It is the pack's first process with more outputs than inputs, and it teaches the central rule of chemistry here.

The rule: if even one output has nowhere to go, the whole unit stalls. You may not want bitumen, but it accumulates anyway, fills its tank and stops the distillation along with the diesel you do want.
Hence the layout: every fraction needs a consumer, a store or a disposal route. Planned ahead, not when it stalls.
And all of them need somewhere to go
Build distillation and route the fractions
industrial_frontier.quest.oil.intro.desc: Oil here is not just fuel. It yields diesel for engines, bitumen for roads, light fractions for chemistry and, in the end, the plastic without which late electronics cannot be built.
That makes the oil line the first production where a layout mistake hits the whole factory at once. Stop the distillation and engines, chemistry and plastics stop with it.
Prospecting and extraction are not instant either: a field has to be found, it is finite, and pumping it takes time. That is deliberate — oil must not be a bottomless barrel next to the base.
industrial_frontier.quest.oil.intro.subt: One feedstock that turns into far too much
industrial_frontier.quest.oil.plastic.de: Diesel feeds engines, the most compact power source of the middle epochs. Plastic goes into electronics, casings and insulation; late circuits cannot be built without it.
Light fractions feed chemistry: solvents, polymers, fertiliser precursors. The oil line joins the chlor-alkali and nitrogen cycles you already walked through in the fourth epoch.
The practical conclusion: you build oil not when you want fuel but when you want plastic. Fuel is a welcome by-product, not the goal.
industrial_frontier.quest.oil.plastic.ti: Where all of it goes next
industrial_frontier.quest.oil.survey.des: A field is found before it is drilled. Samples tell you whether there is oil under a plot and how much — drilling blind is expensive and nearly always pointless.
A well is placed once and for a long time. It takes space, needs power and does not move, so you pick not the nearest spot but the one whose reserve justifies the build.
The reserve is finite. As it drops, the well shifts to residual output: a trickle, but a steady one. Sizing your factory around that trickle is a mistake.
industrial_frontier.quest.oil.survey.tas: Find a field and build a well
industrial_frontier.quest.ops.intro.desc: While the base fitted on one screen there was nothing to take from you. With a mainline, a port, a warehouse and a transit line, a vulnerable point appeared as well.
The outside world reacts to exactly that: operations are triggered by closed contracts and working nodes, not by days lived. The command /if_city_report shows the city indicators.
One rule does not change: every operation has a negotiation window, and none of them destroys your base permanently. Pressure here is a task, not a punishment.
industrial_frontier.quest.ops.intro.subt: Why pressure starts in the fifth epoch
industrial_frontier.quest.ops.intro.titl: Now there is something to cut
industrial_frontier.quest.ops.operations: Convoy escort starts when regular freight begins moving along a leg. The train and its cargo are at stake — track and signals are not destroyed and the depot will release another.
A blockade closes one leg, not the network. Sabotage disables one node of a line without touching the warehouse. A port raid takes the cargo on the quay and one barge.
Joint defence is the only one where your property is not at stake but your reputation is: help an ally or not. Refusing is allowed and does not make the faction an enemy. Details: /if_operations.
Work through what is lost in each operation
industrial_frontier.quest.ops.ordnance.d: The cannon is available early and stays useful: solid shot and grapeshot cost iron, and so does the smoke shell. That is enough to fight back and to learn how the gun works.

The ability to level a fortification — high-explosive, armour-piercing, shrapnel and fluid shells — moved behind steel. By default they too cost plain iron, meaning heavy artillery existed before the industry that explains it.
This is a damage limit, not a ban on the mod. The recipe shapes are unchanged; only the casing material moved.
industrial_frontier.quest.ops.ordnance.t: Understand where the ammunition line is drawn
industrial_frontier.quest.ops.recovery.d: Every operation has a written recovery path, and it is known before it starts. A lost train returns at the depot. A damaged node is repaired normally with its settings intact.
A barge is restored at the quay and the quay remains. After a blockade the leg reopens through a treaty or when the post withdraws — the rails do not go anywhere.
The point is that failure costs time and resources but not the run. The pack does not take away what you built — it makes you build with margin.
industrial_frontier.quest.ops.recovery.s: Recovery is written down in advance
industrial_frontier.quest.ops.recovery.t: Know the recovery path before the operation begins
industrial_frontier.quest.ops.squads.des: The kit of any squad you meet is defined by three things: which faction, which epoch it is in, which role the fighter has. World age and luck do not enter the calculation.
The main consequence: a patrol does not carry what you cannot yet produce, and does not drop it as loot. You cannot skip an epoch through someone else's corpse.
The command /if_squad_loadout lists the roles and their archetypes. The sapper and the gun crew appear only from the fifth epoch — before that the enemy has neither the task nor the reason.
industrial_frontier.quest.ops.squads.sub: Faction, epoch, role — and nothing else
industrial_frontier.quest.ops.squads.tas: Work through the squad equipment rule
industrial_frontier.quest.ops.treaties.d: A treaty is not handed out as a reward and does not sit in your inventory. It is a state of relations that is paid for and that can be lost through behaviour.

A transit pact removes convoy escort and blockade on agreed routes but costs a share of the leg. A port charter removes the raid and obliges you to let other people's barges into the queue on equal terms.
There is a consequence for the neighbours: an alliance with one faction is visible to the rest, and those hostile to it start treating your route as its interest. The list: /if_treaties.
industrial_frontier.quest.ops.treaties.s: It has a price, a term and a consequence
industrial_frontier.quest.ops.treaties.t: Work through the price and consequence of a treaty
Ahead of you is the road from a tent to interplanetary industry. The first era is not about machines, though: it is about deciding where you will build for the next hundred hours.
P0 ends with knowledge, not with an item. You should understand the local climate, know where the nearest vein is, and hold enough food to survive your first mistake.
Picking the wrong spot is not fatal — you can move. But moving costs time, and in this pack time is the real currency.
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.brief.task: Take a look around the world
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.brief.title: Industrial Frontier
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.camp.desc.1: Your first camp does not need to look good. A crafting table, a furnace, a chest and a safe place to sleep are enough.
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.camp.desc.2: The real base comes later, once you know where the veins are, where the water is and where the railway will run. Pouring stone and hours into the first structure is almost always wasted.
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.camp.desc.3: Leave the camp standing: later it becomes a depot, an outpost, or simply a landmark. Nothing has to be torn down.
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.camp.task: Place a crafting table at your camp
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.camp.title: A camp you will not mind leaving
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.exit.desc.1: You have a site, food, a map and your first metal. Repeating the same actions by hand from here is pointless — that is a job for a mechanism.
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.exit.desc.2: P1 introduces rotation as your first production resource: not "faster crafting", but a flow you can measure, overload and repair.
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.exit.task: Move on to the mechanised settlement
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.exit.title: What P1 opens
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.food.desc.1: AppleSkin shows saturation as well as hunger — a second, hidden bar. Saturation is what decides how long before you are hungry again.
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.food.desc.2: In P0 food is gathered by hand: fishing, hunting, a first small plot. That is fine and it is short. Mass catering arrives in P4 together with food chemistry and the city.
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.food.desc.3: Build a small reserve. Eight units is not a lifetime quota, it is insurance against one bad expedition.
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.food.subtit: Food before there is a farm
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.food.title: Field rations
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.loss.desc.1: Gravestone keeps your inventory where you died, and Carry On lets you move chests and machines without dismantling them.
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.loss.desc.2: That is deliberate: the difficulty here comes from designing production lines, not from losing eight hours of work to one cave mistake.
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.loss.desc.3: The safety net is not unlimited, though. A distant grave in a dangerous place still costs time, and sometimes a second death.
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.loss.task: Understand how the inventory safety net works
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.loss.title: Death is a logistics problem
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.map.desc.1: Xaero maps are available from the start on purpose. Finding ore here is a route-planning problem, not a memory test.
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.map.desc.2: Mark your camp, the water and any obvious landmarks. Later the same map will carry veins, the future city and rail corridors.
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.map.desc.3: A good habit: label points immediately. Twenty hours in, "that one cave" will mean nothing at all.
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.map.task: Mark your camp on the map
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.map.title: Mapping the district
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.prospect.de: The usual scattering of vanilla ores is disabled. GregTech generates veins instead: large, rare and tied to stone type and altitude.
That changes prospecting. Instead of digging blindly, follow exposures, caves and ravines, and mark any vein you find — it will last a long time.
Just Enough Resources tells you where each ore occurs. That is a reference, not cheating: this pack does not test your ability to guess.
Collect your first metal. Eight units of raw material is enough to start P1 without a second trip.
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.prospect.ti: Find a vein, not a rock
industrial_frontier.quest.p0.seasons.des: Serene Seasons splits the year into seasons and crops follow them. Anything planted out of season grows slowly or not at all.
For an engineer this means one simple thing: your food line needs either a buffer for the off-season or a greenhouse. Plan it early, not on the first hungry evening.
Check the current season and note how long until the next one. From here on this is a planning input, like voltage or throughput.
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.andesite.de: Andesite alloy is the base part of nearly all early Create. It is cheap, and that is deliberate: this pack does not charge a toll for starting.
Sixteen is a working stock for your first mechanisms, not a quota. Make more once you have automatic feeding.
Note that the alloy yields no material profit. No early recipe in this pack should create metal out of nothing.
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.exit.desc.1: Rotation moves and crushes well, but it does not produce temperature. Without controlled heat there is no steel and no real metallurgy.
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.exit.desc.2: P2 adds a second physical carrier: heat and steam. Mechanics does not go away — it becomes what feeds the boiler and hauls the coal.
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.exit.subtit: Mechanics alone is no longer enough
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.exit.title: What P2 opens
Create does not make crafting faster. It adds a new quantity: rotation, which has both speed and a force budget. You can run short of it exactly as you run short of iron.
This is where the pack's core habit starts: you tune a flow, not a single machine — feed, process, take away, and keep a buffer for failures.
Everything you build in P1 stays useful to the end of the run. Mechanics does not become obsolete, it merely stops being the only tool.
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.intro.task: Understand that rotation is a limited resource
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.intro.title: Why mechanics
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.line.desc.1: Connect source, processing and receiver with a belt. From now on you maintain a line: it has an input, a rate and an output, and any of the three can become the bottleneck.
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.line.desc.2: The most common failure is a blocked output. The machine is not broken, it simply has nowhere to put the result. An output buffer fixes that permanently.
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.line.desc.3: Eight belts is a short working chain, not a decorative conveyor. The point is to see where the line stalls, not to build something pretty.
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.line.task: Assemble a line of at least 8 belts
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.line.title: A line, not a machine
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.mill.desc.1: The millstone is slow and needs nothing but rotation. That is honest early processing: a modest yield in exchange for zero infrastructure.
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.mill.desc.2: Precise metallurgy comes later and will give more. That will not make the millstone useless — it stays the cheap way to cover a small demand.
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.mill.desc.3: This is also where the first automation thought appears: the millstone runs itself, but hand-feeding it every thirty seconds does not.
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.mill.title: Your first processing
A water wheel gives little, but it gives it for free and around the clock. That is enough for your first machines, and in P1 fuel is better spent on the furnace.
The wheel needs flowing water on the correct side. Still water turns nothing — this is the first trap almost everyone hits.
Later rotation will come from steam and engines. The concepts of source, load and headroom stay the same to the end of the game.
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.power.subti: Water is more reliable than it looks
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.power.title: A source of rotation
The mechanical press turns an ingot into a sheet. A sheet is no longer raw material: it is an intermediate that neighbouring systems accept in their recipes.
In this pack a Create sheet and a GregTech plate count as one acceptable form and are taken through a shared tag. What differs is cost and precision, not the material.
This is the first time you produce not for yourself but "to stock for another domain". From here on, almost everything works that way.
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.press.title: The press and the sheet
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.rotation.de: A shaft carries rotation in a straight line, a cogwheel changes direction, a large cogwheel changes speed. Together they form one network with a shared source.
Speed matters: some machines need a minimum RPM and simply will not start on a slow line. That is not a fault, it is a process requirement.
Build a few cogwheels and try turning a line around. A wrong direction is the most common cause of "the machine is idle but everything looks connected".
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.rotation.su: How to read a mechanical line
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.stress.desc: Every machine consumes stress. When total consumption exceeds what the source provides, the entire network stops — not just the newest machine.
The stressometer shows your headroom. Checking it before connecting a new machine saves far more time than diagnosing an already-dead line.
Overload has two fixes: add a source, or split the network. The second is almost always better — independent circuits fail and get repaired separately.
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.stress.subt: Read the instruments, do not guess
industrial_frontier.quest.p1.stress.task: Install a stressometer on your line
industrial_frontier.quest.p2.boiler.desc: A steam boiler turns water into steam and steam into work. Its requirements are simple and strict: continuous water, available fuel and an open outlet.
Breaking any of the three ends the same way. A dry boiler ruptures, a blocked outlet ruptures, and you will be rebuilding more than the boiler.
A rule worth adopting immediately: make the water feed automatic before the first start, not after the first accident.
industrial_frontier.quest.p2.boiler.subt: Water, pressure and one irreversible mistake
industrial_frontier.quest.p2.boiler.task: Learn the requirements of a safe boiler
Brass has a single composition here: three copper to one zinc. Create's stock one-to-one recipe was removed because it contradicted GregTech metallurgy.
Heated mixing replaces it: three copper and one zinc give four ingots. Mass balances, there is no profit, and the output is the canonical GregTech ingot.
This is the template for resolving mod overlaps: do not delete a domain, bring it to an honest material balance.
industrial_frontier.quest.p2.brass.title: One composition for brass
industrial_frontier.quest.p2.carbon.desc: In metallurgy carbon does chemical work: it takes oxygen from the oxide and frees the metal. That is not the same as "burning it for heat".
This is why coal and coke appear in the material passports as their own substance with their own chain, not as furnace consumables.
Build a stock. It goes into fuel, into reduction, and later into chemistry, where carbon becomes feedstock for plastics.
industrial_frontier.quest.p2.carbon.subt: Coal here is not only fuel
industrial_frontier.quest.p2.exit.desc.1: Steam is simple and reliable, but you cannot dose it precisely, move it far without losses, or split it cleanly between consumers. An industrial district needs more.
industrial_frontier.quest.p2.exit.desc.2: P3 introduces electricity as measurable, distributable energy — together with voltage, amperage and the cable discipline you will have to respect.
industrial_frontier.quest.p2.exit.title: What P3 opens
A normal furnace does one thing: heat an item until it is done. Industry needs something else — a target temperature, a hold time and atmosphere control.
Three branches grow from this at once: reducing metal with carbon, making steam as an energy carrier, and alloys that simply do not exist in vanilla.
P2 is the first era where a mistake is expensive. A boiler without water and a blocked steam outlet is not "suboptimal", it is an explosion.
industrial_frontier.quest.p2.intro.subti: Why the furnace stops being enough
industrial_frontier.quest.p2.intro.task: Understand the difference between a furnace and a process
industrial_frontier.quest.p2.intro.title: Heat is a process
industrial_frontier.quest.p2.ore_route.d: Create's stock ore crushing is disabled. It offered a second, cheaper way to the same metal and devalued GregTech metallurgy entirely.
The correct route has two steps across two domains: mechanical beneficiation makes a concentrate, precise processing extracts metal and by-products from it.
The curated recipes for that route arrive together with the full GregTech form registry. Until then plain smelting applies, rather than a hand-stretched substitute.
The principle is worth learning now: a by-product is not waste, it is feedstock for a neighbouring line, and in P4 it becomes mandatory.
industrial_frontier.quest.p2.ore_route.s: Why the cheap route is closed
industrial_frontier.quest.p2.plates.desc: A plate can come from a Create press or from a GregTech machine. The pack accepts both through a shared tag, but that does not make them equal.
Create gives volume cheaply and visibly. GregTech gives precision and fits chains where purity matters. The choice depends on where the part is going.
This is how the whole domain federation works: not "which mod is better", but which process is physically appropriate at this step.
industrial_frontier.quest.p2.plates.task: Obtain 8 iron plates by either route
industrial_frontier.quest.p2.steam_machi: A GregTech steam machine has a steam inlet, a material input, a product output and its own interface. The sides are not interchangeable — check that first.
Start a new machine on one small batch. That shows you the real cycle time and consumption instead of an assumption.
If it will not start, the checklist is almost always the same: is there steam, is the output free, is it connected on the right side, is the input the right material.
Run one batch on a steam machine
Steel is iron with a precisely held carbon content. Hence the process requirement: not just heat, but controlled time and atmosphere.
Steel becomes the basis of nearly everything that follows: machine casings, pipes, rails and the first electrical installations. You will need a lot of it.
Four ingots is a teaching batch. It proves the route works; you will scale it later with automatic feeding.
industrial_frontier.quest.p2.steel.subti: Your first alloy that vanilla does not have
industrial_frontier.quest.p2.steel.title: Steel
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.bridge.desc: The pack allows GregTech energy to be exported as FE, but not taken back. Reverse converters are disabled on purpose.
The reason is simple: a pair of opposing converters almost always forms a loop where energy grows. That destroys the point of having power systems at all.
The same rule will hold for every future network — steam, nuclear and the strategic circuit. A bridge is allowed, a ring is not.
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.bridge.subt: Energy must not travel in a circle
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.bridge.task: Confirm there is no FE to EU return path
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.bridge.titl: EU and FE: a one-way bridge
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.buffer.desc: An industrial district draws unevenly: machines switch on in bursts and create peaks a lone generator cannot absorb.
An energy buffer smooths the peaks and gives you reserve while the generator is serviced. Without it, any pause in fuel stops the whole line.
You already saw the same principle on the belt in P1: buffers at the input and the output are not waste, they are what makes a line stable.
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.buffer.task: Place a buffer between generator and network
A cable has a voltage rating, a current rating and a loss per length. Exceeding the first two destroys the cable; the third simply eats part of your energy.
Hence the practical rule: short thick runs from generator to node, thin runs from node to machines. One long line "to everything" is the classic early mistake.
Cable insulation is not decoration: bare wire loses more and is dangerous on contact. In this pack that is a deliberate part of the balance.
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.cable.subti: A wire is a rated part too
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.cable.task: Size a run by voltage and current
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.cable.title: Cable, losses and burnout
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.exit.desc.1: You have a site, mechanical processing, heat, steel and an electrical district that runs without manual labour. That is the complete P0–P3 vertical slice.
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.exit.desc.2: Chemistry comes next: fluids, gases, return streams and by-products you cannot simply discard. With it arrives the city and its standing demand.
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.exit.desc.3: The main thing to carry out of these four eras: difficulty here lives in designing flow, not in the number of identical clicks.
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.exit.subtit: What you can do now and what comes next
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.exit.title: Closing the slice
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.generator.d: The generator is where the previous era turns into the next one. Everything you built in P2 now feeds an electrical network.
Start with one generator and one consumer. That shows real output and draw instead of a datasheet estimate.
Headroom matters more than peak output: a network running at its limit stops the moment you add one machine.
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.generator.t: Run a generator and a single consumer
GregTech distinguishes voltage, current and total energy. Voltage is an equipment class, current is how many consumers pull at once, EU is the energy itself.
Most early accidents come from the first one: feeding a receiver above its class burns it out rather than making it run faster.
The good news is that the rules are few and constant. Understand them once at LV and you will read every later tier the same way.
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.intro.subti: Three quantities you must not confuse
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.intro.title: Electricity as discipline
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.line.desc.1: Build a chain that runs without you: material feed, processing, product removal and a buffer for when the receiver stalls.
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.line.desc.2: That is the proof you have mastered the era. Not the number of machines, but no longer needing to stand there moving items.
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.line.desc.3: If the line stops, diagnosis is the same as in P1 plus energy: is the voltage right, is the cable overloaded, is the output free.
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.line.task: Run a line that needs no hand feeding
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.line.title: Your first electric line
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.machine.des: An electric machine is built from a casing, a circuit and parts of its class. The class decides what voltage it accepts and what it can do.
Machines of one generation share an interface layout: input slots, an output slot, energy, and side configuration. Learn one and you can read the whole row.
Stock up on steel plates — they are the most common casing part, and making them in batches beats making them one machine at a time.
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.signal.desc: Redstone appears here in two entirely different roles: as a control signal and as a chemical material for electronics.
Do not conflate them. The signal controls when a machine runs; the material decides what it is made of. Later the second role matters far more than the first.
Collect a working stock — you will need it both for district automation and for your first electronic components.
industrial_frontier.quest.p3.signal.subt: And only after that a material
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.chlorine.de: Electrolysis of brine yields chlorine, hydrogen and alkali at once. All three are useful, and all three appear together — you cannot opt out of one.
This is the best example of why chemistry cannot be planned around a single product. If you only want chlorine, the hydrogen and alkali still have to go somewhere.
Chlorine goes to water treatment and polymers, hydrogen back into ammonia, alkali into soap, processing and acid neutralisation. The circle closes on earlier chapters.
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.chlorine.ta: Find a consumer for all three products
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.contract.de: A contract is an honest sink for bulk resources and proof that production works. It must not be a hidden tax, so its content is known up front.
Early contracts are simple: district plumbing, a housing block, a food reserve. Each takes materials by category and in batches, not by hundreds of clicks on one block.
The reward is a permit, a service, a blueprint or a convenience. It never creates a resource from nothing and never skips the main line.
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.contract.ta: Accept and close one utility contract
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.exit.desc.1: You have water, acids, fertiliser, food and a city that consumes all of it. The problem is no longer producing — it is delivering without losing things on the way.
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.exit.desc.2: P5 adds regional scale: bulk processing, railways, ports and the AE2 digital warehouse, which finally opens together with its own industrial chain.
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.exit.title: What P5 opens
Fertiliser makes harvests more predictable but does not cancel the season. Serene Seasons still decides what grows when; chemistry only smooths the dips.
Organic compost is the early rung: it is made from kitchen and farm waste, closing the same loop as sludge from water treatment.
Industrial fertiliser will come from the nitrogen line and give more. That will not obsolete compost: it stays the cheap way to cover a small need.
So far you moved items. Now fluids and gases appear, and they behave differently: you cannot put them in a chest, they only flow where a route exists, and they run out quietly.

The second difference matters more. A chemical process almost always has a by-product, and you cannot discard it: every stream needs a receiver. Otherwise the line stops from a full output, not from missing input.
The third is return. Solvents, acids and coolants work in a loop. Closing the loop beats producing them again, but the loop must have losses and make-up.
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.intro.task: Understand how a fluid line differs from an item line
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.intro.title: Chemistry starts with water
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.kitchen_bat: Create: Central Kitchen automates Farmer’s Delight recipes using Create machinery you already have. That matters: there is no second catalogue of kitchen machines in this pack.
Yield does not increase — what changes is that you no longer stand at the pot. Exactly as the millstone in P1 gave no extra ore, it removed a repeated action.
Run one automatic batch and compare it with the manual one. The difference is time and attention, not food per unit of input.
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.kitchen_man: Farmer’s Delight gives you a knife, a board, a stove and a cooking pot. That is enough to feed an expedition and to see what a dish is actually made of.
The manual kitchen stays in the game forever as the quick way to cook a little. It does not become obsolete — it stops being the only option.
Build a cooking pot and run one full cook. You will be automating this exact process next, and knowing it by hand helps.
Craft a cooking pot and cook a dish
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.nitrogen.de: Nitrogen is taken from air, combined with hydrogen into ammonia, oxidised into nitric acid, and from there into fertiliser, explosives and rocket chemistry.
One chain feeds three entirely different industries. That is the point of the chemical city: you build the line once and it has several consumers.
Note the order: fertiliser comes before explosives not for story reasons, but because the city needs food first and agronomy pays the line back sooner.
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.nitrogen.ta: Follow the chain from ammonia to fertiliser
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.rations.des: The city consumes a few standard rations, and each accepts a category through tags rather than one specific dish. Nobody forces you to cook a particular soup.
Variety is rewarded with bonuses and contracts, not punished by penalties. There is no thirst, no mandatory spoilage and no competing nutrition bars here — that is deliberate.
A ration needs drinking water. That is exactly why the treatment plant at the start of this chapter was a prerequisite for civic growth, not a detour.
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.rations.sub: Variety instead of a mandatory menu
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.raw_water.d: The pack distinguishes three waters. Raw is what you scoop with a bucket: fine for cooling and construction, not for drinking and not for precise chemistry.
Technical water has been filtered: its composition is predictable, and only it is accepted by chemical processes. Drinking water passes one more stage and appears only after treatment.
This is a gate, not paperwork. City rations require drinking water specifically, so treatment has to run before the settlement starts growing.
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.raw_water.s: Three different waters in one world
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.raw_water.t: Fill a bucket with raw water
Raw water is not drinking water
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.sewage.desc: Sewage splits further: sludge goes to compost or biogas, and the cleaned fraction returns to the loop as process water.
The return is deliberately bounded. Some water is always lost to evaporation and washing, so raw make-up is permanent and a perpetual loop does not exist.
This is where the waste fields in the substance passports start to make sense. Every stream in this chapter later becomes an input for agronomy, biogas or chemistry.
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.sewage.subt: Waste is feedstock for a neighbouring line
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.sewage.task: Give every sewage stream a receiver
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.sulfur.desc: Sulfuric acid is the workhorse of industrial chemistry. Etching, batteries, ore processing and fertiliser all need it, which is why it comes first.
The feedstock is sulfur from minerals and from cleaning petroleum fractions. The process needs technical water, so treatment comes before it, not alongside it.
The acid is hazardous and recoverable. You close its loop rather than dumping it: that is safety, economy, and the first real return stream in your factory at once.
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.sulfur.task: Trace the sulfuric acid route in JEI
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.treatment.d: A treatment plant takes raw water and splits it into three streams: technical water, drinking water and mandatory sewage. The third is not optional — it always appears.
Hence a design rule: count outputs before you build. A line planned around its main product only will clog with sewage on the first batch.
Buffer every output. It is the same trick as the buffered belt in P1, except now an overflow stops the whole utility node, not one machine.
industrial_frontier.quest.p4.treatment.t: Plan the split into three streams
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.ae2_autocra: The crafting unit is the moment the network starts assembling instead of you. It costs an HV sensor — a whole epoch after you got storage.
The gap is deliberate. Between seeing everything in one list and having the system do everything lies real distance, and you cross it with infrastructure, not with a single recipe.
The accelerator that lets several jobs run at once costs another epoch — EV. Without it autocrafting still works, just one job at a time.
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.ae2_channel: An ME cable does not carry unlimited connections. A normal cable carries eight channels, a dense one thirty-two, and every device occupies one channel along the whole path back to the controller.
Hence the classic first outage: the network worked, you added a ninth device, and half of it went dark. Nothing broke — that segment simply ran out of channels.
There are two cures: a controller with separate branches leaving it, and dense cable on the trunk. The rule is simple — count channels at the narrowest point, not across the whole network at once.
Channels: why the network went dark
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.ae2_entry.d: The digital factory opens with three blocks: the charger makes charged quartz, the inscriber prints processors, the energy acceptor lets current into the network. All three cost steel and MV electronics — there is nothing to build them from earlier.
At first you only get storage and a terminal. That is already a lot: chests stop being a maze and finding an item takes a second.
The network cannot craft for you yet. That is deliberate: if everything arrived at once, trains and pipes would lose their value the same evening.
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.ae2_pattern: A pattern is a written-down recipe: what to put in, where to send it, what to expect back. The pattern provider holds it and hands the job to a machine when work appears.
Priority decides where the network puts a result. A cell reserved for metal gets a higher priority, so metal does not spread across shared disks but sits where you look for it.
The same priority saves you from overflow: give the cheapest bulk item its own low-priority cell and it will not eat the expensive space.
The network learns what goes where
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.ae2_recover: An ME network goes down for three reasons, and all three are fixed by diagnosis, not reinstallation. First — it ran out of power: look at the acceptor and the buffer, not at the cables.

Second — it ran out of channels: count the devices on the narrow segment. Third — a craft is jammed: a job is waiting for an item that exists neither in the network nor in the pattern, and it waits forever.
Hence a design rule: keep a physical buffer at critical machines. If ME stalls, the line should finish its shift on its own stock instead of stopping outright.
Know the three causes of a network outage
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.balance.des: The honest question of the epoch: if an ME network can pull anything from anywhere, why keep trains at all? The answer is in the limits, not in preference.

ME removes the drudgery of searching and counting. It does not create material, does not cross distance for free, and goes dark together with the power. A train moves mass cheaply, works without a network and is visible from outside.

That is why ME here opens with storage only, autocrafting is held back an epoch, and contracts demand a physical reserve. The goal is that by the end you have both a terminal and a mainline — not a terminal instead of one.
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.balance.tas: State where ME ends and haulage begins
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.bulk_proces: Mass processing is not a bigger crusher. It is a decision about who in this pack may get more metal out of an ore than it visibly contained.
There is one such owner: GregTech. Only its chain separates crushed, washed and purified, returns by-product minerals and explains where the gain came from.

So the ore branch of the Immersive Engineering crusher and arc furnace is gone: 67 recipes handed out doubled metal on a parallel ladder. Everything else in IE stayed — scrap melting, alloys, the press, the sawmill, the excavator. The mechanical bridge is Create's crushing wheels, and it is honest: strictly one to one, no gain.
Understand why ore multiplication belongs to one mod
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.contracts.d: Regional contracts differ from municipal ones in one way: they test not a batch but the ability to hold a flow. Delivering once is not enough.
The throughput pledge asks for a declared rate and a reserve in case of a stop. Manual topping-up does not count — production holds the flow, not the player.

The closure pledge asks for the same flow with nothing dumped: packaging comes back, by-products are accepted, district pollution does not grow. The command /if_regional_contracts shows the terms and the reward in advance.
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.contracts.s: Flow and closure instead of a one-off delivery
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.contracts.t: Work through the two new contract classes
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.freight_rai: Freight between districts moves by train. Track, signal, station and schedule are a separate engineering problem: where the passing loop goes, where the buffer sits, what happens when two trains ask for one section.
A mainline is built once and serves for a long time, so rails are worth producing in series rather than laying one at a time.
The second railway from Little Logistics was removed on purpose: three parallel railways mean three translations, three recipe sets and one and the same job.
Until now everything fitted into one glance: the furnace next to the mine, the kitchen next to the field, the store two steps away. The fifth epoch breaks that compactness — ore in one place, chemistry in another, the city in a third.
So distance appears. And distance is not decoration: it has to be carried, guarded and paid for. Four transport layers are built here, and each answers for its own job.

The mainline carries freight. The transit line carries people. Water carries the heavy and the liquid. The last mile carries to the door. No layer replaces another — that is the point of this chapter.
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.intro.subti: What changes in the fifth epoch
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.intro.task: Understand why the epoch needs four different transports
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.intro.title: The district is no longer a dot
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.last_mile.d: Between the station and a particular machine there is always a stretch a train will not cover. That is the last mile, and it eats more time than it looks like.
Funnels, belts, pipes, vehicles and the field kit work here — the toolbox that travels with the crew to the line under construction.
The rule is the same as above: do not drag a trunk-route solution into a district. A train for twenty blocks is expensive and slow.
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.last_mile.s: From the station to the door
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.reserve.des: A fifth-epoch warehouse does not hold everything — it holds enough for the moment the line stops: one shift of work without deliveries. That is the long-term reserve.
The food part returns to the cycle: a vegetable crate opens back into exactly nine units, the same number that went in. Packaging you cannot return is not accepted into a city contract.
Check yourself with a simple question: if the mainline stops for a day, does the city survive or stop with it?
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.reserve.sub: A store that survives an outage
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.transit_lin: A city without passenger transport is a warehouse with residents. An MTR line ties the housing district, the industrial zone and the terminal together with a timetable instead of a random sprint.

Entry to the system costs steel and MV electronics. By default the rail node was made of iron and logs — meaning a metro could be built on day one, before the city, before electricity and before the very idea of a district.
The passenger network carries no freight. That is not a mod limitation but a division of roles: mixing people and crates loses the point of both.
industrial_frontier.quest.p5.water_route: A river and a coastline are a ready-made trunk route you do not have to build. A tug pulls a string of barges along guide rails; the dock loads and unloads.
Water wins where cargo is heavy, cheap and not urgent: gravel, ore, liquids. It loses on speed and on the fact that geography chooses the route.
So water does not compete with rail, it completes it: a port is the node where one leg becomes another.
industrial_frontier.quest.p6.alloys.desc: The second entry machine does what makes a dedicated metallurgy necessary: alloys that hold neutron flux, temperature and pressure at the same time.

Ferroboron absorbs and keeps its shape. Tough alloy goes into casings. Zirconium becomes fuel cladding — and swapping it for a cheap metal is not allowed, or the whole point of fuel preparation disappears.
From here the domain is self-sufficient in structural materials and no longer depends on borrowed parts.
The station is handed to the city when the loop is closed: a reactor with thermal margin, an exchanger, a turbine, condensation, a cooling store, backup power for its own needs and radiation monitoring around the perimeter.
The reward is not an item. The city's base load moves to the station, and power stops being the bottleneck for every other industry at once.
The command /if_nuclear_contract shows the terms, the reward and the refusal condition. The refusal is simple: a station that dumps heat or spent fuel outside is not accepted.
industrial_frontier.quest.p6.dosimetry.d: Radiation cannot be seen, heard or felt in time. The first sign of a mistake is a number on an instrument, not how you feel. That is why the counter is built before the reactor, not after.
Shielding is three things: distance, time and a barrier. Lead and concrete always work; a suit works only while it is intact.

The command /if_nuclear_safety holds the whole procedure: measurement, shielding, storage, emergency shutdown and decontamination. It is not about caution in general but about this mod's actual mechanics.
industrial_frontier.quest.p6.dosimetry.s: The one sense humans do not have
Isotopes of one element are chemically identical — no reaction will separate them. Only mass will, and the difference is a fraction of a percent.
Hence the centrifuge, and hence the price: enrichment costs incomparably more energy than any earlier purification step.
And hence the depleted remainder. It is not rubbish: it has its own role in shielding and in late alloys, so it does not go to the dump.
Separation by mass, not by chemistry
By default the first NuclearCraft machine costs lead, flint and a piston — meaning the whole nuclear industry would open in the first epoch, before steel, before electricity and before the city.
Here it costs steel plates, a voltage coil, an electric motor and an HV machine hull. That is the sixth epoch and nothing earlier.

The lock sits on exactly two machines — this one and the alloy smelter. Everything else in the mod is built from them, so all 4331 recipes were left alone: close the entrance and you close the domain.
industrial_frontier.quest.p6.entry.subti: Entry costs steel and HV electronics
industrial_frontier.quest.p6.entry.title: The domain's first machine
industrial_frontier.quest.p6.fuel.desc.1: Enriched material is pressed into pellets, pellets are stacked into zirconium cladding, the cladding becomes a fuel cell. Every step exists for one reason: to keep fission products inside.
industrial_frontier.quest.p6.fuel.desc.2: The first load may be assembled by hand — exactly once, to understand how it works. After that a line does it: this pack will not make you hand-build a dozen assemblies for every refuelling.
industrial_frontier.quest.p6.fuel.desc.3: A finished cell is already dangerous. From this point the dosimeter stops being a formality.
industrial_frontier.quest.p6.fuel.title: Fuel fabrication
industrial_frontier.quest.p6.heat_loop.d: A reactor does not produce electricity. It produces heat, and everything else is a way to carry that heat to a turbine without losing it or letting it out.

The loop is closed: coolant takes the heat, the exchanger passes it to water, water becomes steam, steam gives its energy to the turbine and condenses back. There is no free coolant discharge in this pack — not into a river, not into the air.
Hence the city contract's requirement: a station that dumps heat outside is not accepted by the city.
Until now power was mined: burn coal, spin turbines, run cable. There was never enough, and that was a clear, familiar limit.

A reactor removes that limit entirely. One station covers the base load of the city and every industry at once — and in exchange brings the first machine in this pack that punishes carelessness with the loss of a district rather than the loss of resources.
So this chapter is not build-and-switch-on. First the substances, then purification, then measurement and shielding, and only then startup. Order matters more than speed here.
industrial_frontier.quest.p6.intro.task: Understand how a reactor differs from a generator
industrial_frontier.quest.p6.intro.title: Power stops being the problem
industrial_frontier.quest.p6.isotopes.de: Isotopes are not mined. They come from irradiating targets in a running reactor and separating the result — meaning only whoever keeps a station has them.
This is the only legitimate route to several late materials, and it cannot be bypassed: factions do not sell mandatory fuel isotopes, that trade route is closed.
A surplus beyond your own needs is visible to the outside world. What follows from that is in the operations chapter.
industrial_frontier.quest.p6.isotopes.su: What only a reactor can give you
industrial_frontier.quest.p6.materials.d: The nuclear industry does not rest on uranium. It rests on the materials that control the reaction: graphite slows neutrons, boron absorbs them, beryllium reflects them, zirconium holds the fuel in cladding, lithium and fluorite carry the heat.
Without them uranium is just a heavy metal. That is exactly why passports for these six substances were written before the reactor was opened.

Graphite is the first point where early metallurgy feeds the nuclear industry directly: it is made from the carbon of the second-epoch coke line, not mined. Reactor purity differs from technical, and an ordinary coal block will not become a moderator.
industrial_frontier.quest.p6.materials.s: And none of them is fuel
industrial_frontier.quest.p6.purificatio: Between uranium ore and something you can load into a reactor lies the whole chemistry of the fourth epoch: leaching, precipitation, purification and conversion into a compound fit for separation.
This is not a formality. At every step part of the mass leaves as tailings, and tailings do not vanish — they are accounted for exactly like the effluent of the water line.
The practical conclusion is the same as in the Academy of Elements: never take purity higher than the next step requires. Extra refining is spent energy and extra waste.
Follow the route from ore to compound
industrial_frontier.quest.p6.reactor.des: A reactor is not a block but an assembly: casing, fuel cells, moderator, absorbers and heat removal. It runs while the heat produced stays below the heat removed, and not a minute longer.
So heat removal is calculated before startup, not added once the temperature climbs. Thermal margin is exactly the difference between a power station and an accident.

The first reactor is built by hand from this chapter. After that the Multi Builder Tool automates rebuilding identical multiblocks — this pack will not make you place a hundred blocks by hand a second and third time.
industrial_frontier.quest.p6.reactor.sub: Heat removal is designed before startup
A spent assembly is not empty. Fissile material remains, fission products have accumulated, and new elements have appeared that barely exist in nature.
First the cooling pond: freshly unloaded fuel is too active to handle and must stand. Then reprocessing returns what is usable to the cycle and sends the rest to long-term storage.
This is what closing the cycle means. Without it the station still runs but becomes a warehouse of problems — and the city contract demands a cooling store on site.
Fuel does not run out, it changes
